first_impression.reaction: My daughter sent this because she's got her heart set on peonies and I said 'in what month?'. The first line says exactly that: start with the date, not a mood board. It's calm and sensible, no gushing. I'll read it through.

journey.quote: Choosing wedding flowers in season starts with a date, not a mood board.
journey.reaction: Thank you. That's what I've been trying to tell her. I'll be reading that line out at dinner.

journey.section: Why choose wedding flowers in season
journey.quote: Petals hold their shape, stems drink well, and arrangements last through a long evening rather than tiring by the speeches.
journey.reaction: That's the practical reason I care about. If I'm paying for flowers I want them looking right at nine o'clock, not wilted by the toasts.

journey.section: Wedding flowers in season in Australia by month
journey.quote: What grows well in a given month varies with the region, the grower and the year, so the month notes below are about the conversation rather than a fixed list.
journey.reaction: Fair enough, and honest. I did half expect a list of flowers under each month from the heading, but a list of sensible questions to take to the florist is probably more use to me in the end.

journey.quote: Ask whether the venue has water and shade for buckets during the day, and whether a bouquet can be kept chilled until the moment you leave for the ceremony.
journey.reaction: The sort of thing nobody thinks of until it's too late. A Melbourne January can be forty degrees. Good.

journey.quote: Ask about scale too: in a smaller winter room, a few generous arrangements can carry more presence than many small ones.
journey.reaction: Sensible spending advice dressed up nicely. Fewer, better pieces. I approve.

journey.section: Spring in September, October and November
journey.quote: Waratah flowering is concentrated in spring, and growers have worked to stretch its season to reach peak demand periods such as Christmas. ([AgriFutures Australia](https://agrifutures.com.au/related-projects/farm-based-methods-for-control-of-flowering-in-waratahs/))
journey.reaction: Nice to see an Australian flower get a mention, but the bracketed name stuck on the end of the sentence reads like a footnote in a government report. It broke my reading.

journey.quote: For a couple, that is the florist's and importer's work, not yours.
journey.reaction: Good. The paragraph before was getting a bit Department of Agriculture for me, but this line tells me plainly I don't need to worry about it. That's reassuring.

journey.quote: Agree in writing which flowers are essential to you and which the florist may substitute.
journey.reaction: In writing. That's the phrase I look for. If someone swaps the roses for something cheaper, I want it on paper beforehand.

journey.quote: Resist the urge to pack flowers from home.
journey.reaction: My sister would absolutely have tried that. Useful.

journey.quote: Ask them the same three questions: what is local, what is brought in, and what the backup is.
journey.reaction: Fine for the flowers, but if it's a florist in Italy, I'm the one wondering what we're paying, in what currency, and what's written down. The article goes quiet on that here, just when it matters most to me.

journey.section: Planning your flowers and spend with your florist
journey.quote: An imported stem, a flower at the edge of its season or a date in a peak week can change a quote, and so can scale, labour and set-up.
journey.reaction: Straight talk about what pushes the price up. I like that it doesn't pretend flowers are cheap. I'd want the quotes laid out so I can see those things line by line.

journey.section: Planning your flowers and spend with your florist
journey.quote: With Wedded Concierge, you have one Wedded Advisor, start to finish, as a single point of contact, and your advisor confirms inclusions in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: One named person and things in writing. That's the paragraph I'd forward to my husband.

unanswered_questions: Does a Wedded Advisor help with a wedding here in Melbourne, or only overseas? The closing says 'anywhere in the world' but the article is mostly about Australian weddings.
If the wedding is abroad, who helps us find a florist at the destination we can trust with a deposit?
Is the first step a phone call with a real person before anything is paid?
What does the Wedded Advisor cost, and is that agreed in AUD before work starts?
Who do I ring if the flowers don't turn up on the morning of the wedding?

turn_offs_found.quote: Ask them the same three questions: what is local, what is brought in, and what the backup is.
turn_offs_found.why: For an overseas florist, the questions I lose sleep over are about the deposit, the currency and what's in writing. The article is careful about writing things down elsewhere but doesn't say it here, where it matters most.

turn_offs_found.quote: Waratah flowering is concentrated in spring, and growers have worked to stretch its season to reach peak demand periods such as Christmas. ([AgriFutures Australia](https://agrifutures.com.au/related-projects/farm-based-methods-for-control-of-flowering-in-waratahs/))
turn_offs_found.why: The bracketed source tacked on the end looks clumsy on the iPad and 'peak demand periods' is trade talk. Minor, but it's the one spot that didn't read smoothly.

would_share_with: My daughter, with the opening line about the date before the mood board and the three questions (local, imported, backup)
My husband, with the cost paragraph and the line about the Wedded Advisor confirming inclusions in writing

cta_reaction.quote: A Wedded Advisor plans venue, travel, vendors and payments, anywhere in the world, so the flowers sit within a plan that already fits your date and your destination.
cta_reaction.why: 'Payments' caught my eye, because that's my side of it. But this is a flowers article and we haven't settled on overseas or at home yet. I'd click if the wedding goes abroad, and I'd want to speak to someone on the phone before anyone takes a deposit.
